title: Episode 113: John Adams and the Quasi-War: Standing Alone for Peace
description:
In 1798 and 1799, President John Adams faced the XYZ Affair, war hysteria, and treason within his own cabinet. Defying Alexander Hamilton and the High Federalists, Adams sacrificed his political career to secure peace with France, preserving the infant American Republic.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the presidency of our second chief executive, John Adams, during the volatile, storm-tossed years of seventeen ninety-eight to eighteen hundred, to witness one of the greatest acts of presidential courage and political martyrdom in American history: the Quasi-War with France. Caught in the crossfire of the Napoleonic wars, American merchant ships were being plundered on the high seas by French privateers. When French diplomats demanded humiliating bribes in the notorious XYZ Affair, war fever swept across the United States. Alexander Hamilton and Adams's own treasonous cabinet demanded a full-scale declaration of war and the creation of a massive standing army. But President Adams understood that a full war with revolutionary France would bankrupt the young republic, tear the nation apart, and destroy the Constitution. Standing entirely alone, Adams defied his party, his cabinet, and his friends to dispatch an emergency peace mission to Paris, averting war at the price of his own presidency. Here is George with the full, gripping story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: CAUGHT IN THE CROSSFIRE OF EMPIRES
When John Adams was inaugurated as the second President of the United States in March seventeen ninety-seven, succeeding the monumental figure of George Washington, he inherited an international crisis that threatened to strangle the young American republic in its cradle. Across the Atlantic, the French Revolution had mutated into an all-consuming total war between revolutionary France and the monarchical coalition led by Great Britain. The United States, possessing a vast commercial merchant fleet but virtually no navy, found itself trapped like a wooden rowboat caught between two colliding battleships.
France was enraged by the seventeen ninety-four Jay Treaty, an Anglo-American trade agreement that Paris viewed as a treasonous betrayal of the seventeen seventy-eight Franco-American alliance that had won American independence. In retaliation, the French Directory unleashed hundreds of heavily armed privateers across the Caribbean and the Atlantic. In less than two years, French corsairs seized over three hundred American merchant ships, confiscating millions of dollars in cargo and beating American sailors in island ports.
Desperate to avert war, President Adams immediately dispatched an extraordinary three-man peace commission to Paris: Charles Cotesworth Pinckney of South Carolina, John Marshall of Virginia, and Elbridge Gerry of Massachusetts. Adams was determined to maintain Washington's policy of strict neutrality, knowing that the fledgling United States—with no professional army, no standing navy, and a fragile federal union—could not survive a full-scale war against the greatest military power in Europe. President Adams wrestled with conflicting diplomatic cables in Philadelphia, determined to protect American merchant shipping without courting war.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE INSULT OF THE XYZ AFFAIR
Arriving in Paris in October seventeen ninety-seven, the American envoys were met with breathtaking imperial arrogance and contempt. France's cunning, corrupt foreign minister, Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord, refused to receive the American ministers officially. Instead, Talleyrand dispatched three secretive French intermediaries—designated in secret diplomatic dispatches simply as Agents X, Y, and Z: Jean-Conrad Hottinguer, Pierre Bellamy, and Lucien Hauteval.
The French agents delivered an extortionate, insulting ultimatum: before formal negotiations could even commence, the United States must issue a formal apology for speeches made by President Adams, grant France a massive low-interest loan of thirty-two million Dutch guilders, and pay an upfront cash bribe of two hundred and fifty thousand dollars directly into Talleyrand's personal pocket.
The American envoys were stunned by the brazen corruption. When Agent X pressed for the money, warning that the French fleet would ravage the American coastline if denied, General Pinckney delivered the legendary, fiery retort: 'No! No! Not a sixpence!' The negotiations collapsed, and Pinckney and Marshall demanded their passports to return home, while Gerry remained in Paris in a desperate bid to prevent an immediate French declaration of war. French privateers operated with near-total impunity across Caribbean waters, seizing American cargo and terrorizing peaceful merchant crews.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE FEVER OF WAR SWEEPS AMERICA
In March seventeen ninety-eight, President Adams received the decoded dispatches from Paris detailing the extortionate demands. Recognizing that concealing the insult would invite charges of weakness, Adams submitted the redacted documents to Congress, christening the scandal the 'XYZ Affair.'
The release of the dispatches detonated an unprecedented explosion of patriotic fury across the United States. The rallying cry swept through town halls and newspapers from Boston to Savannah: 'Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute!' Anti-French hysteria reached a fever pitch; citizens wore black cockades in their hats, sang patriotic ballads like 'Hail Columbia' in taverns, and burned effigies of French leaders in city squares. The Federalist Party, which had long championed a pro-British, anti-French foreign policy, saw an extraordinary political opportunity to crush their domestic political rivals, the pro-French Democratic-Republicans led by Vice President Thomas Jefferson.
Congress moved decisively on a war footing. It formally revoked all treaties with France, created the Department of the Navy, authorized the construction of twelve heavy warships, and authorized the recruitment of a ten-thousand-man provisional standing army. On the high seas, an undeclared naval war—known to history as the Quasi-War—erupted across the Caribbean and the Atlantic, as newly commissioned American frigates like the USS Constellation began hunting down French privateers. Patriotic rallies echoed across American city squares as citizens contributed private funds to construct naval frigates for the defense of the republic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TREASON IN ADAMS'S CABINET
Yet John Adams's greatest and most dangerous enemies were not across the Atlantic in Paris; they were sitting at his own cabinet table in Philadelphia. In a misguided effort to maintain political unity following George Washington's retirement, Adams had made the fatal mistake of retaining Washington's cabinet officers: Secretary of State Timothy Pickering, Secretary of War James McHenry, and Secretary of the Treasury Oliver Wolcott Jr.
Unbeknownst to Adams, all three cabinet secretaries were secretly loyal not to the President, but to his bitter political rival: Alexander Hamilton. Hamilton, leading the radical 'High Federalist' faction of the party, was consumed by grandiose military ambitions. Hamilton envisioned using the war with France to raise an immense standing army under his own command, which he planned to march south to conquer Spanish Florida and Louisiana, or even invade Mexico and South America in a spectacular campaign of imperial conquest.
Even worse, Pickering, McHenry, and Wolcott operated as Hamilton's spies within the executive branch. They leaked private presidential memoranda to Hamilton, sabotaged Adams's diplomatic initiatives, and systematically concealed critical foreign intelligence reports from the President. Hamilton used his influence to force Adams to appoint him as major general and second-in-command of the army under the aging Washington, effectively establishing an armed, rival military power center outside presidential control. Hamilton's faction envisioned using the expanding army to consolidate executive power and expand American borders through foreign conquest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SEDITION ACTS AND THE THREAT OF TYRANNY
During the summer of seventeen ninety-eight, caught in the grip of wartime paranoia and partisan hysteria, the High Federalist majority in Congress passed the notorious Alien and Sedition Acts: four draconian laws that represented the darkest assault on civil liberties in early American history. The Naturalization Act extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years to disenfranchise immigrant voters; the Alien Acts authorized the President to deport any non-citizen deemed dangerous to the peace and safety of the country without a trial.
Most tyrannical was the Sedition Act, which made it a high federal crime punishable by fines and imprisonment to write, print, utter, or publish 'any false, scandalous, and malicious writing' against the government, Congress, or the President. Federalist prosecutors weaponized the act ruthlessly, indicting dozens of Republican newspaper editors, printers, and even an outspoken Republican congressman, Matthew Lyon of Vermont, who was thrown into a freezing jail cell for criticizing President Adams.
While Adams signed the legislation under intense party pressure, he refused to enforce the Alien Acts and grew increasingly sickened by the authoritarian drift of his party. Adams recognized that Hamilton and the High Federalists were eager to provoke a full-scale declared war with France not merely to defend national sovereignty, but to permanently entrench a standing army, silence domestic opposition, and subvert the constitutional republic. The draconian provisions of the Sedition Act aroused deep public outrage, inspiring Thomas Jefferson to author the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE THUNDERBOLT FROM QUINCY
In late seventeen ninety-eight, while resting at his farm in Quincy, Massachusetts, alongside his brilliant wife and trusted advisor Abigail Adams, the President received secret, reliable intelligence through diplomatic backchannels in the Netherlands. France's newly risen leader, Napoleon Bonaparte, had overthrown the corrupt Directory and had no desire for war with America. Talleyrand sent official, secret assurances that if the United States dispatched a new minister, he would be received with all the respect due to the representative of a great, free, and independent nation.
Adams faced the supreme moral crossroad of his life. If he yielded to Hamilton and declared full war, he would ride the crest of popular war hysteria to an easy, landslide re-election in eighteen hundred, cementing Federalist dominance for a generation. But Adams knew that war would bankrupt the nation, trigger armed rebellions in Virginia and Kentucky, and potentially destroy the American Union. Conversely, if he sent a peace mission, the High Federalists would brand him a coward and traitor, split the party, and destroy his political career.
Without consulting a single member of his treacherous cabinet, President Adams made his historic move. On February eighteenth, seventeen ninety-nine, he dropped a political bombshell that stunned the nation: he sent a message to the United States Senate formally nominating William Vans Murray as minister plenipotentiary to France to negotiate peace. The Federalists in Congress were incandescent with fury; Secretary of State Pickering openly contemplated refusing to deliver the diplomatic credentials. But Adams held his ground with granite stubbornness, threatening to resign and leave the presidency to Vice President Thomas Jefferson if the Senate refused to confirm his peace commissioners. Adams's courageous decision to send a second peace commission defied the unanimous advice of his party, prioritizing peace over personal glory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PEACE OF MORTEFONTAINE AND THE MARTYRDOM OF ADAMS
In May eighteen hundred, having discovered the depth of their treachery, President Adams decisively purged his cabinet, firing Secretary of War James McHenry in a blistering confrontation and dismissing Secretary of State Timothy Pickering. Adams dispatched his peace commissioners across the Atlantic, where they were received with lavish royal honors by First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte.
On September thirtieth, eighteen hundred, the historic Treaty of Mortefontaine—the Convention of eighteen hundred—was officially signed at Joseph Bonaparte's country estate. The treaty formally terminated the seventeen seventy-eight alliance, ended the Quasi-War on the high seas, restored mutual commercial trade relations, and avoided a ruinous trans-Atlantic war that would have devastated the young American nation.
The political cost to John Adams was immediate and total. Enraged by the peace treaty, Alexander Hamilton published a vicious fifty-four-page pamphlet attacking Adams's character, sanity, and fitness for office, fatally fracturing the Federalist Party. In the election of eighteen hundred, Adams was defeated by Thomas Jefferson. Adams packed his trunks and departed Washington in the early morning darkness, returning to his humble farm in Quincy as a rejected, one-term president.
Yet history has vindicated John Adams as a towering statesman of unyielding moral integrity. By standing entirely alone against his party, his cabinet, and popular hysteria, Adams kept the infant American Republic out of the Napoleonic slaughterhouse, allowing the fragile Constitution time to take deep root. Late in life, John Adams looked back upon that lonely decision with serene, justifiable pride, writing: 'I desire no other inscription over my gravestone than: Here lies John Adams, who took upon himself the responsibility of the peace with France in the year eighteen hundred.' It stands as one of the greatest profiles in presidential courage in the history of the world. The historic Convention of eighteen hundred secured American neutrality on the high seas, allowing the young republic to grow into a global commercial power.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
John Adams requested that his tombstone carry only one inscription: 'Here lies John Adams, who took upon himself the responsibility of the peace with France in the year eighteen hundred.' I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey with our third President, Thomas Jefferson, and the Corps of Discovery across the uncharted wilderness to the Pacific Ocean.
